name: Evenki
confidence_why: Nedjalkov's 1997 reference grammar, the only full description available, states that Evenki stress is not fixed but predictable from the shape of the word (long vowels attract it, and in words of short vowels it falls toward the end) while admitting that the system needs more study; Morozova, Osipov and Androsova 2023 likewise treat a long first-syllable vowel as the stressed one, and the only different picture, Tsumagari 2009's initial stress with a weight-sensitive high pitch, describes Solon of Inner Mongolia, which its author regards as a separate language.
catalog_citation: Nedjalkov, Igor. 1997. Evenki. (Descriptive Grammars.) London/New York: Routledge. [archive.org item 361-evenki, scanned book; StressTyp2 cites it as 1996]
catalog_locator: section 3.3.2.1 and 3.3.2.5, pp. 316-318 (pp. 336-338); morphophonology of stress 3.5.1.2-3.5.1.3, p. 323
catalog_quote: it is possible to state that stress in Evenki is not constant: its position in different words (and word forms) may vary from the first to the last syllable. ... Position of stress is predictable in terms of the phonotactic structure of the concrete word. In words consisting of two syllables with two short vowels, stress may fall either on the first syllable (e.g. 'ulle 'meat', 'ollo 'fish') or more often on the second syllable (e.g. bi'ra 'river' ...). If a word or a word form has more than two syllables with short vowels the stress falls on the last syllable ... e.g. giram'na 'bone', baka'ran 'he found' ... If a disyllabic word has either a long vowel or a cluster of consonants in the middle of the stem then the stress falls on the first syllable, e.g. 'hul-la 'blanket', ... 'hal-ka 'hammer', 'i:-kte 'tooth', ... 'sa:-ren '(s)he knows'. In a disyllabic word with two long vowels the st…
sweep_summary: Evenki (even1259) is in the catalog as weight-hedged on Nedjalkov 1997. the list of works with stress in the title has one item, Morozova & Androsova 2019 'Intonacija voprosov v rechi amurskih evenkov: osnovnoj ton' (Theoretical and Applied Linguistics 5(4):84-96). Crossref resolved it to DOI 10.22250/2410-7190_2019_5_4_84_96, which redirects straight to the open PDF on lingua.amursu.ru; downloaded, (text intact, alongside, logged). It is an instrumental study of pitch contours of general vs wh-questions in Amur (Eastern) Evenki (rise on the last syllable for yes/no questions, fall with nucleus on the verb for wh-questions) and says nothing about word-stress placement: relevance prosody-but-not-word-stress, silent on the catalog. To look for a better first-hand statement I also read the on-disk material: Morozova et al. 2023 (unstressed vowels) defers to Konstantinova 1960/1964 for the Evenki stress rules and, second-hand, places stress on a first-syllable long vowel or on a non-initial short vowel in its examples (consistent with weight-hedged); new scanned of the Vasilevich 1948 contents pages (pp. 346-356) shows no stress section anywhere in the book, and Bulatova 1999's phonetic-features section (pp. 16-21) has none either. altaica.ru's Tungusic library has no Konstantinova; that grammar is the high-priority acquisition. the best new statement: none found; the catalog's Nedjalkov 1997 coding stands.

new_statements.quote: Usually the vowel of the first syllable is stressed and pronounced clearly, while the short vowel on and after the second syllable tends to be reduced and sometimes dropped in casual speech. A high pitch, on the other hand, falls either on the last syllable (if the syllable contains VV or final C) or on the penultimate syllable (otherwise). If we admit the pitch pattern of a word as such, we can partly resort to it, in its turn, to decide the phonological shape of a word.
new_statements.citation: Tsumagari, Toshiro (2009). A sketch of Solon grammar. Journal of the Graduate School of Letters 2. pp. 1-21.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (extracted text of the HUSCAP PDF, 22 pp incl. cover, text intact). Sec. '2.4 Accent and vowel reduction' begins at line 171 (book p. 3) and continues on p. 4 after the running header; the quoted three sentences are there word for word ('Usually the vowel of the first syllable is stressed and pronounced clearly, while the short vowel on and after the second syllable tends to be reduced and sometimes dropped in casual speech.' / 'A high pitch, on the other hand, falls either on the last syllable (if the syllable contains VV or final C) or on the penultimate syllable (otherwise). If we admit the pitch pattern of a word as such, we can partly resort to it, in its turn, to decide the pho…
new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record for Evenki (qs-tier-2026-09-12) has an empty rule and there are no existing statements, so this is the first placement statement held by the project. It applies to SOLON (Solon Ewenki of Hulun Buir, Inner Mongolia), which Glottolog's hh.bib files under evn ('language code = {Solon = Evenki [evn]}'), but which the author himself says 'should be regarded as a separate language (i.e. Solon), not as a dialect of Siberian Ewenki' (p. 1). It should not be entered as the rule for Siberian/literary Evenki without a Solon qualifier.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Two separate word-level prominences in Solon: (a) stress is on the first syllable ('usually'), whose vowel is pronounced clearly, while short vowels in the second and later syllables reduce or drop in casual speech; (b) independently of stress, a high pitch sits on the final syllable when that syllable is heavy (long vowel VV or closed by a consonant), otherwise on the penultimate syllable, i.e. a weight-sensitive right-edge pitch peak. The author uses this pitch pattern as a diagnostic of a word's phonological shape.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed as such; the right-edge high pitch (final if heavy, else penult) is presented as a pitch phenomenon separate from the initial stress.
new_statements.exceptions: 'Usually' hedges the initial-stress statement; recent loanwords (especially Chinese) are said at the head of sec. 2 to show exceptions to the inherent phonology; vowel reduction/dropping of non-initial short vowels is limited to casual speech.
new_statements.identity_note: Tsumagari 2009 describes Solon (Solon Ewenki, Ewenki Autonomous Banner, Hulun Buir, Inner Mongolia; some speakers in the Nonni basin of Heilongjiang), based on Poppe 1931, Hu & Chaoke 1986, Chaoke 1995 and the author's own observation. Glottolog files it under even1259 (hh.bib language code 'Solon = Evenki [evn]'), but the author states it is generally classified as a separate language from Siberian Evenki. Bulatova & Grenoble 1999 describes the (Siberian) Evenki literary language; its stress page was not readable.

readall_conflicts: No source-vs-source disagreement could be tested: the only placement statement read is Tsumagari 2009 on Solon (first-syllable stress plus a weight-sensitive final/penult high pitch), and the stress section of Bulatova & Grenoble 1999 (sec. 2.3, p. 5, on Siberian/literary Evenki) is absent from every open Rosetta excerpt. The one tension is internal to Tsumagari's description: stress (initial) and high pitch (right edge, weight-sensitive) are placed differently, so a catalog reading that keys on pitch rather than stress would come out 'weight-sensitive' rather than 'fixed: initial syllable'.

audit.reasoning: Quote confirmed verbatim in the Nedjalkov 1997 text we hold at the cited sections/pages. The deciding source is the standard English reference grammar and the same primary every database uses; the 'weight-hedged' coding faithfully mirrors the author's own hedge ('Much basic research.. is required') plus his long-vowel/medial-cluster conditions. Open-access material downloaded now (Morozova/Androsova 2018, 2019, 2023, 2025; Vasilevich 1948; Bulatova 1999, all is silent on stress placement or defers to Konstantinova 1964; nothing found contradicts the record. The record is not 'well-sourced' only because the deeper Russian primary (Konstantinova 1964) and the instrumental monograph (Andreeva 1988) are unread and print-only; if either is obtained, a re-read could firm up (or drop) the weight analysis, but no reclassification is indicated now

sources.citation: Morozova, O. N., Osipov, B. Ya. & Androsova, S. V. (2023). Bezudarnyj vokalizm v evenskom i evenkijskom jazykakh [Unstressed vowels in Even and Evenki]. Teoreticheskaja i prikladnaja lingvistika 9(2), 120-130. doi:10.22250/24107190_2023_9_2_120
sources.quote: Безударные позиции гласных определялись согласно правилам расстановки ударения, представленным в работах по эвенскому [Лебедев, 1978 ; Новикова, 1991] и эвенкийскому языкам [Константинова, 1960]. [p. 120] ... Редукции подвержены безударные гласные непервых слогов, следующих за первым слогом, содержащим долгую гласную фонему. ... В результате образуется цепочка следующих друг за другом безударных слогов с редуцированными гласными при доминировании долгого гласного первого ударного слога. [p. 121] ... Например, онʹóкŏл 'напиши, нарисуй', оллокōнмŏ 'рыбку', олóдʹŏнŏ 'идя вброд', хójвŏ 'болото', олóнŏ 'испугались' ... гласный о с диакритическим знаком «акут», обозначает ударный гласный слога. [p. 122] — ENG: Unstressed positions were determined by the stress-placement rules given for Evenki in Konstantinova 1960. ... Reduction affects unstressed vowels of non-initial syllables following a first syllable containing a long vowel phoneme ... a chain of unstressed reduced syllables dominated by the long vowel of the first, stressed syllable. ... in the examples the acute marks the stressed vowel.
sources.note: Second-hand only: it defers to Konstantinova (1960/1964) for the stress-placement rules and does not restate them; it describes stress as sitting on a first-syllable long vowel when there is one, and its cited Konstantinova examples mark stress on a non-initial short vowel in words without one (онʹóкŏл, олóдʹŏнŏ, олóнŏ, хójвŏ). Consistent with the catalog's 'position varies, predictable from phonotactic (weight) structure' coding but adds no first-hand rule.

sources.citation: Morozova, Olga N. & Androsova, Svetlana V. (2019). Intonacija voprosov v rechi amurskih evenkov: osnovnoj ton [The prosody of questions in the Amur Evenks' speech: Pitch]. Teoreticheskaja i prikladnaja lingvistika / Theoretical and Applied Linguistics 5(4), 84-96.
sources.quote: В ходе эксперимента установлено, что для опознания вопросительности в общих вопросах на эвенкийском языке существенно инклинационное интонирование последнего слога. Для специальных вопросов характерно понижение тона на глаголе. Эти результаты расходятся с экспериментальными данными, полученными ранее Н. Я. Булатовой и Л. Гренобль (1999 г.) об инклинации на начальном участке с вопросительным словом в специальных вопросах. [p. 84] — ENG: The experiment established that for recognising interrogativity in Evenki general questions the rising intonation of the last syllable is essential. Special questions are characterised by a fall in pitch on the verb. These results diverge from the earlier experimental data of N. Ya. Bulatova and L. Grenoble (1999) on a rise on the initial stretch with the question word in special questions.
sources.locator: pp. 84 (abstract), 87, 95 (conclusion); 13 pp., sections 1 Введение, 2 Акустический анализ, 3 Заключение
sources.note: Nothing about word-stress placement. The paper is an instrumental (PRAAT) study of F0 contours of yes/no, clarifying and wh-questions in the Eastern (Amur, Selemdzha/Zeya) dialect from 11 speakers: general questions = rise on the last syllable of the syntagm; wh-questions = fall with the nucleus on the verb. The only occurrence of 'ударн-' (p. 87) is a quotation of T. M. Nikolaeva on prosodic strong points in general ('акцентногенны, т. е. потенциально ударны'), not a statement about Evenki word stress.
